units.title: Reading Russian that was not written for learners: news reports, rule sheets, personal voice, numbers and unstated meaning

lessons.title: Reading a news report: what happened, who says it, and what the writer thinks
lessons.explanation: A news report is usually the first real Russian text a learner meets outside a course, and it is the easiest kind of text to misread, because the grammar of reporting is built to make claims sound like facts. The discipline of this lesson is to read every report by answering three questions in a fixed order. First: which event is being asserted? Second: who is asserting it? Third: where does the writer's own evaluation appear? Russian answers the third question with words that look like observations. Take сообщение (sa-ap-SHCHYE-nee-ye), 'a report, an item of news' — the noun for the genre itself — and сообщается (sa-ap-SHCHA-ye-tsa), 'it is reported', an impersonal reflexive verb with no stated subject, which lets a paper announce a claim while leaving the speaker of that claim unnamed. A source is an источник (ees-TOCH-neek), 'source', and when a paper leans on an institution rather than a person, the source is often a представитель (preed-sta-VEE-tyel), 'representative', a person whose accountability belongs to the organisation behind him. The phrase по данным (pa DAN-nym), 'according to the data', hands an assertion to a document, exactly as 'according to' does in English. A citation is a ссылка на (SSYL-ka na), 'a reference to', and the place where reports hide weak evidence is precisely where the ссылка points to another publication, издание (eez-DA-nee-ye), 'publication', rather than to the original document. Evaluation hides in three further items. Очевидно (a-chee-VEED-na), 'evidently', presents an inference as if it were a perception. Подчеркнуть (pad-cherk-NOOT), 'to emphasise', tells you that the writer endorses the emphasis being reported. Комментарий (ka-men-TA-reey), 'comment', locates a statement in a speaker's mouth: a commentary is something someone said, not something that happened, and a sentence built on it can be true even when what was said is false. The headline, заголовок (za-ga-LO-vak), must be read separately, because it is written by a different person from the reporter, it is often not a full sentence, and it routinely asserts more than the article will support. Finally, word order does part of the work. Cornell's Beginning Russian Grammar states the rule plainly: 'The general rule for Russian word order is to put new information at the end of the sentence.' The same page adds that the speaker can stress the subject in initial position in speech, but that 'in written Russian that auditory option is not available, so the pseudo-passive construction (Object+Verb+Subject) is very commonly used.' That construction is why a Russian news sentence can end on the surprising element — the number of roubles, the name of the ministry, the date — while the actor sits in the middle. Read reports with a pencil: mark the event, mark every attribution, and underline every word you could not defend in front of the person being described.
lessons.example: Here is an authored teaching report, written for this lesson and not quoted from any newspaper: Вчера городская администрация сообщила, что с первого сентября стоимость проезда в метро вырастет на пять рублей. По данным городского департамента транспорта, рост тарифа связан с обновлением подвижного состава. Однако представители профсоюза водителей подчеркнули, что зарплаты сотрудников остаются на прежнем уровне. Очевидно, что обсуждение бюджета продолжится на следующей неделе. Как сообщает издание «Городские новости» со ссылкой на источник в мэрии, окончательное решение ещё не принято. (fchee-RA ga-rad-SKA-ya ad-mee-nee-STRA-tsee-ya sa-ap-SHCHEE-la, shto s PYER-va-va seen-tyab-RYA STO-ee-mast PRA-yez-da f meet-RO VY-ras-tyet na pyat ROOB-lyey. pa DAN-nym ga-rad-SKO-va dee-par-TA-men-ta TRAN-spar-ta, ROST TA-ree-fa SVYA-zan s ab-nav-LYE-nee-yem pad-VEEZH-na-va sa-STA-va. ad-NA-ka preed-sta-VEE-tee-lee prap-sa-YU-za va-DEE-tye-ley pad-cherk-NOO-lee, shto zar-PLA-ty sa-TROOD-nee-kaf as-ta-YUT-sya na PRYEZH-nyem OO-rav-nye. a-chee-VEED-na, shto ab-soozh-DYE-nee-ye byu-DZHE-ta pra-dal-ZHEET-sya na SLYE-doo-yoo-shchey nee-DYE-le. kak sa-ap-SHCHA-yet eez-DA-nee-ye ga-rad-SKEE-ye NO-vas-tee sa SSYL-kay na ees-TOCH-neek f MEH-ree-ee, a-kan-CHA-tyel-na-ye ree-SHYE-nee-ye ye-SHCHO nye PREET-sya-ta.) Now read the three questions against it. Question one, the events: the fare will rise by five roubles on 1 September (sentence 1); the rise is linked to fleet renewal (sentence 2); staff pay has not changed (sentence 3); the budget discussion will continue (sentence 4); the final decision is pending (sentence 5). Question two, the sources. Sentence 1 attributes the event to городская администрация, a named institution, through the reporting verb сообщила — accountable, checkable. Sentence 2 attributes the stated cause to a document, городской департамент транспорта, through по данным — accountable to a text, not a person. Sentence 3 attributes the pay claim to представители профсоюза водителей — a party with an interest, and however announces that the writer is not neutral. Sentence 4 has no attribution at all: очевидно is the writer's own inference dressed as perception, and the future verb продолжится makes it a prediction rather than a report. Sentence 5 is the weakest link in the text — как сообщает издание «Городские новости» со ссылкой на источник в мэрии — a publication citing an unnamed official, so nothing in that sentence can be traced or contested by anyone the reader can reach. Question three, the writer's stance: however, очевидно and подчеркнули. The extractable summary is therefore three paid-for claims and two weak ones, and the difference between them is visible only in the attribution phrases, not in the assertions themselves.
lessons.question: In the model report, which sentence asserts something while naming no source that the reader could trace?
lessons.answer: Sentence 5 — Как сообщает издание «Городские новости» со ссылкой на источник в мэрии — because it cites a publication citing an unnamed official, so no identifiable person or document stands behind the claim.
lessons.distractor: Sentence 4 — Очевидно, что обсуждение бюджета продолжится — because очевидно means that the claim is unproven, so it has no source.
lessons.correction: Sentence 4 is not untraceable, it is unsourced on purpose: очевидно is the writer's own inference and the writer is the identifiable person who made it, so it can be quoted back to them. Sentence 5 is different in kind: the attribution chain ends in источник в мэрии, 'a source in the mayor's office', which names nobody. A general-grammar test tells the two apart: an unsourced judgement still belongs to the writer, while a chain of attributions can leave a claim belonging to no one in particular — and that is where a careful reader stops and writes 'we cannot check this'.

depth.definitions: A report (сообщение) is a text whose central sentences assert that something is the case. Attribution is the part of a sentence that names who or what stands behind the claim: a person, an institution, a document, or nobody. Evaluation is the part that carries the writer's stance: evidently, importantly, unfortunately, or a verb such as подчеркнуть. A hedge is a word that reduces the writer's commitment to a claim, and Russian does this with по данным when the basis is a text, and with по мнению plus a genitive source when the basis is a person. A pseudo-passive is the Russian word order Object+Verb+Subject, which lets written Russian place the new, interesting element last. Prerequisites: this lesson assumes the close-reading routine of lesson 81 (claim, support, stance and their discourse markers), the register contrast of lesson 82, the impersonal and passive constructions of lesson 83, the verbal nouns of lesson 84, and the case system taught in lessons 31-70, because по данным requires the dative plural, ссылка на requires the accusative, and сообщается is built on a reflexive ending. If any of those feel thin, reread lesson 83 before continuing.
depth.mechanism: Why does reporting grammar work this way? Because information structure is grammar, not style. Russian marks what is already known by putting it early and what is news by putting it late, and written Russian cannot fall back on intonation to rescue a sentence, so it uses the pseudo-passive instead. The impersonal сообщается removes the actor from the syntax, which is not the same as removing the actor from the world: someone filed the report, and the paper's editors stand behind it even when the sentence does not say so. The same logic explains по данным: the dative phrase makes a document the grammatical basis of the claim, which is a stronger commitment than an anonymous source, because a named document can be requested. Two limits matter. First, attribution is evidence about where a claim came from, not evidence that the claim is true; a named ministry can be wrong. Second, a chain of attributions can be grammatically complete and epistemically empty, as sentence 5 of the model shows; English-language journalism treats this as a question of objectivity, understood as an institutional ideal rather than a guarantee, since objective reporting is meant to 'portray issues and events in a neutral and unbiased manner, regardless of the writer's opinion or personal beliefs'. Whether a given paper meets that ideal is not decidable from one paragraph, and nothing in this lesson should be read as a claim that any specific outlet is or is not reliable.
depth.secondExample: Read a second, contrasting text — a company announcement, also authored for this lesson. Компания «Северный дом» сообщает о переходе на новые тарифы с 1 октября. По данным отдела продаж, средний счёт за год снизился на восемь процентов. Однако независимые эксперты сомневаются в методике расчёта. (kam-PA-nee-ya SYE-veer-ny DOM sa-ap-SHCHA-yet a pee-ree-KHO-dye na NO-vy-ye ta-REE-fy s PYER-va-va akt-yab-RYA. pa DAN-nym at-DYE-la pra-DAZH, SRYED-nee SHCHOT za got snee-ZEEL-sya na VO-seem pra-TSEN-taf. ad-NA-ka nee-za-VEE-see-my ex-PYER-ty sa-mnee-VA-yut-sa f mee-TA-dee-kye ras-CHO-ta.) The verb of doubt here is сомневаться (sam-nee-VAT-sa), 'to doubt, to be sceptical', and it governs a prepositional phrase: сомневаться в чём-то, in what. The contrast with the news report is instructive in three places. First, the accountable source is the company itself — Компания «Северный дом» сообщает — so the announcement is the company's own speech act, not a report about an event; a reader who treats it as news has confused a press release with reporting. Second, the second sentence attributes a figure to an internal department, отдел продаж, which is a party to the transaction being described; the phrase по данным does not make a number neutral, it names whose numbers they are. Third, the third sentence does what careful reporting does: it asks whether the method behind the number holds up, эксперты сомневаются в методике расчёта. Notice also that sentence 2 contains a box construction of the kind Cornell calls 'a word or phrase which is boxed in by an adjective and the word it modifies' — in средний счёт за год снизился the prepositional phrase за год sits inside a noun phrase built on счёт, and a word-for-word English rendering ('average bill for year decreased') is not English. You must find the noun the box belongs to before you can decide what decreased.
depth.mistake: The commonest misconception at this level is that a report has a factual first half and an opinionated second half, so that everything before the first obvious judgement word can be trusted. Russian reporting does not arrange itself that way. In the model text the strongest attribution appears in the first two sentences and the weakest in the last, while the only sentence with no source at all sits in the middle. A second, related misconception is that очевидно is a neutral signal of obviousness; it is a claim of obviousness, and it can be challenged like any other claim, because the writer chose it instead of writing по данным or со ссылкой на. Diagnostic procedure: take any sentence and ask which words would have to be deleted to make the sentence unattributable — if the answer is 'none, because there is no attribution', you have found the writer speaking in their own voice; if the answer is a chain of two attributions, you have found a claim that is nobody's to defend. A learner who marks both cases as 'information' has not yet separated the two roles that a sentence in a report can play.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Choose a Russian news item of at least four sentences (the readings below point to material you can use, or use any short report you can reach). Build a three-column table with one row per sentence: column one, the event asserted; column two, the attribution, quoted verbatim, including the case of the dependent noun; column three, any evaluation marker. Then write an English summary of at most seventy words in which every clause is attached to its source, using the form 'according to X, ...' or 'the ministry claimed that ...'. Model response for the last two sentences of the model text: event — the budget discussion will continue; attribution — none, the writer's inference, signalled by очевидно; evaluation — очевидно itself, plus the future tense продолжится. Event — the final decision is pending; attribution — издание «Городские новости» citing источник в мэрии, an unnamed source; evaluation — none stated, but the hedge окончательное ... ещё не принято reduces commitment. Written summary: 'According to the city administration, the metro fare will rise by five roubles on 1 September, a change the transport department links to fleet renewal. Union representatives said pay has not changed. The newspaper Городские новости, citing an unnamed source in the mayor's office, reports that no final decision has been taken; the writer expects the budget discussion to continue, which is the writer's inference rather than a reported fact.' Self-review rubric, four points: (1) every clause names its source or explicitly says 'unnamed'; (2) no evaluation marker is smuggled into the reported claims; (3) the two sentences whose only basis is the writer's inference are marked as such; (4) you can point to the exact Russian words that support each clause. Score yourself one point per criterion and reread any row that scored zero before moving on.
depth.summary: Reading a Russian report is not translating sentences in order; it is reconstructing a small network in which each assertion hangs from a source. The grammar that carries this network is ordinary Russian grammar used for a purpose: impersonal reflexive verbs such as сообщается, dative phrases such as по данным, genitive after ссылка, and the pseudo-passive word order that puts the news at the end of the sentence. Because the same forms appear in advertising, government notices and press releases, the skill transfers directly to every written genre you will meet, including the announcements and instructions of the next lesson. The transferable habit is the three-question routine: event, source, stance — applied sentence by sentence, with a pencil, before any translation is attempted.

visual.title: Four-stage attribution audit of one news report
visual.description: A labelled sequence of four reasoning stages applied to the five-sentence model report, each stage producing a written artefact. Rendered as text steps, not as video or animation.
steps: Stage 1 — Sentence split. Number every sentence and write beside each number only the clause that could be true or false (the event or state). Output: five one-line event statements.

Stage 2 — Attribution extraction. For each sentence copy the exact attribution words (сообщила, по данным, подчеркнули, со ссылкой на) with the noun that follows in its grammatical case. Output: a source column in which each entry is a person, an institution, a document, or the word 'none'.
Stage 3 — Chain test. Where a source is itself a text or a publication, follow the chain one link back and write who, if anyone, ends it. Output: a mark of 'traceable' or 'unreachable' per sentence.

Stage 4 — Stance marking. Underline every participant-evaluation word (однако, очевидно, подчеркнули) and label it as inference, emphasis, or contrast. Output: a stance column, then a seventy-word summary in which each clause carries its source label.

lessons.title: Reading rules and instructions: obligation, prohibition and the administrative register
lessons.explanation: Instructions and rules are the second large family of real Russian texts, and they are written in a register that deliberately removes people from the grammar. A learner who reads an инструкция (een-STROOK-tsee-ya), 'a set of instructions', as if it were a conversation will miss both the obligations and the loopholes. Five devices carry almost all of the meaning. First, the impersonal predicatives with a dative person: необходимо (ne-ap-kha-DEE-ma), 'it is necessary', and следует (SLYE-do-eet), 'one should', take an infinitive and, when a person is mentioned at all, put that person in the dative: посетителю необходимо ..., 'the visitor must ...'. Second, the pair разрешено (raz-ree-shye-NO), 'it is permitted', and запрещено (za-pree-shchee-NO), 'it is forbidden' — past passive participles used as fixed predicatives, so impersonal that they rarely name anyone. A third form, допускается (da-poos-KA-ye-tsa), 'it is allowed, it is permitted (by the rules)', is more common inside rule books than either of them and usually signals a concession rather than a right. Third, the conditional prepositions: в случае (f SLOO-cha-ye), 'in the event of', takes the genitive, and при необходимости (pree ne-ap-kha-DEE-mas-tee), 'if necessary', is a fixed phrase that behaves as an adverb. Fourth, согласно (sag-LAS-na), 'according to, in accordance with', takes the dative, not the genitive, which is the single most common reading error in this register: согласно правилам, not *согласно правил. Fifth, the emphatic formula of a public notice, убедительная просьба (oo-bee-DEE-tyel-na-ya PROS-ba), 'an insistent request', followed by an infinitive: убедительная просьба не курить, 'please do not smoke'. Notice what is missing from that formula and from the whole register: no ты or вы, no imperative directed at a named person, and almost no active first-person verb. Obligation is stated as a property of the situation. The word обязательно (a-bya-ZA-tyel-na), 'mandatorily, without fail', is the one plainly graded word in the set, and it is worth circling whenever you see it, because it marks the rule the writer actually intends to enforce. Aspect matters here rather than in narrative: a prohibition written with the imperfective describes a standing rule, while the same prohibition with the perfective can describe a single occasion, which is why Cornell's grammar says to use the imperfective with нельзя 'unless you're talking about the impossibility of getting something done on a specific occasion'. And не надо must be read with care, because the same page warns that it 'can mean either mustn't/shouldn't or don't have to, but the usual interpretation is mustn't/shouldn't', while the unambiguous way to say 'you don't have to' is можно не plus an imperfective infinitive.
lessons.example: Here is an authored notice of the kind found in a Russian reading room; it is a teaching text, not a quotation. Правила пользования читальным залом. Вход в зал — по читательскому билету. Сумки и верхнюю одежду необходимо оставить в гардеробе. Согласно правилам библиотеки, посетителям не разрешается проносить в зал еду и напитки. При необходимости сотрудник может выдать временный пропуск. Не допускается выносить книги из зала без отметки. Убедительная просьба соблюдать тишину и не курить на территории библиотеки. В случае утери билета необходимо обратиться в администрацию. (PRA-vee-la PAL-za-va-nee-ye chee-TAL-nym ZA-lam. fkhot f ZAL pa chee-TA-tyel-ska-moo bee-LYE-too. SOOM-kee ee VYERKH-nyu-yu a-DYEZH-doo ne-ap-kha-DEE-ma as-TA-veet f gar-dee-RO-bye. sag-LAS-na PRA-vee-lam beeb-lee-a-TYE-kee, pa-see-TEE-tye-lyam nye raz-ree-SHA-ye-tsa pra-na-SEET f ZAL ye-DOO ee na-PEET-kee. pree ne-ap-kha-DEE-mas-tee sa-TROOD-neek MO-zhet VY-dat vree-MYEN-ny PRO-poosk. nye da-poos-KA-ye-tsa VY-na-seet KNEE-gee ee ZA-la byez at-MYET-kee. oo-bee-DEE-tyel-na-ya PROS-ba sa-blyu-DAT TEE-shee-noo ee nye koo-REET na tye-ree-TO-ree-ee beeb-lee-a-TYE-kee. f SLOO-cha-ye oo-TYE-ree bee-LYE-ta ne-ap-kha-DEE-ma a-bra-TEET-sa v ad-mee-nee-STRA-tssee-yoo.) Read it four ways. As obligations: what a visitor must do is в гардеробе оставить сумки (necessary), обратиться в администрацию (necessary), соблюдать тишину (an insistent request that functions as an obligation). As prohibitions: проносить еду (не разрешается), выносить книги без отметки (не допускается), курить (не курить inside the просьба). As permissions: получить временный пропуск (может, a discretionary power of the staff, not a right of the visitor — a distinction the register does not spell out). As conditions: вход только по билету, and the whole final obligation is conditional on losing that ticket. Now look at the grammar of the obligations themselves. Two sentences put an infinitival predicate first and a genitive noun last — в случае утери билета — which is exactly the box construction of lesson 91: утери belongs inside the в случае phrase, and a word-for-word rendering ('in case of loss of ticket') produces clumsy English. Two sentences use the dative: посетителям не разрешается, which names the person the prohibition binds, and that dative is the only human presence in the sentence. Every other obligation is subjectless. Finally, notice the morphology: не разрешается and не допускается are reflexive passives built on the same -ся ending that сообщается used in the news report of lesson 91. The rule-book register and the reporting register share this device, and they use it for the same purpose — to state a norm or an event while leaving the actor unnamed.
lessons.question: A notice says: Не надо выносить книги из зала. Which reading is the safe one for a reader deciding what to do?
lessons.answer: The usual reading is a prohibition — 'you must not take books out of the reading room' — because Cornell's grammar states that не надо 'can mean either mustn't/shouldn't or don't have to, but the usual interpretation is mustn't/shouldn't'; a reader treating a rule as binding should adopt the stronger reading and look for confirmation elsewhere in the document.
lessons.distractor: Не надо means 'you do not have to', so the sentence merely reports that no obligation exists and taking books out is neither forbidden nor required.
lessons.correction: That is the second reading, and it is the one that misleads learners, because the same page notes that the unambiguous way to express 'don't have to' is a form of мочь with не before an imperfective infinitive, as in можно не выносить. Since the notice uses не надо rather than можно не, the prohibition reading is the default; and in a rule book the practical asymmetry matters — if you are wrong in the permissive direction you break a rule, if you are wrong in the prohibitive direction you only ask for clarification.

depth.definitions: Register is the set of grammatical and lexical choices a text makes for a social purpose; the administrative-official register, официально-деловой стиль, is the written register of rules, laws, contracts, notices and official correspondence. Obligation is the meaning 'must'; prohibition is 'must not'; permission is 'may'; no-necessity is 'need not'. Russian marks these with three different kinds of device: impersonal predicatives with an infinitive (необходимо, следует, нельзя, можно), short adjectives that agree with a nominative subject (должен, должна, должны), and reflexive-passive verbs (разрешается, не допускается). The person bound by an impersonal obligation appears in the dative; the person bound by должен appears in the nominative. Prerequisites: the dative of the recipient in lesson 61, the impersonal sentences of lesson 62 (мне нужно, мне холодно), the modal and command material of lesson 69, the aspect contrast between narrative and instruction in lesson 85, the verbal nouns of lesson 84 — necessary because rule books are built on them — and the case government of prepositions from lessons 53 and 61.
depth.mechanism: Why is this register built out of impersonal devices? Because a rule must be repeatable by anyone and enforceable against anyone, so the grammar suppresses the individuals. The Wikipedia article on официально-деловой стиль lists exactly these features: 'сжатость, компактность изложения' (compression, economy of language), 'стандартное расположение материала, нередкая обязательность формы' (a standard arrangement of material and an obligatory form), 'повествовательный характер изложения, использование номинативных предложений с перечислением' (narrative presentation and nominative sentences listing items), 'прямой порядок слов' (predominant direct word order), 'тенденция к употреблению сложных предложений' (a tendency to complex sentences) and 'почти полное отсутствие эмоционально-экспрессивных речевых средств' (an almost total absence of emotional and expressive means). Each of those features is visible in the model notice: the list of permitted and forbidden objects, the nominalised вынос книг, the direct order inside each clause, the complex sentences with в случае and согласно, and the absence of any expressive word except убедительная. The mechanism creates a real reading risk, however. Because the register presents every statement as a standing fact, it flattens the difference between rules the institution must follow and rules the institution has chosen, and between rights of the visitor and powers of the staff. That difference is not recoverable from the grammar alone; it is recoverable only by asking who has the authority to change the sentence — which is why the lesson insists on parsing может as a discretionary power rather than a permission granted to you.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the notice with a spoken procedure written at a workplace, also authored for this lesson. Слушай, порядок такой: сначала возьми заявку у клиента, потом проверь паспорт, а данные внеси в систему до конца дня. Если паспорта нет, ничего не оформляй — отдай заявку старшему. (SLOO-shay, pa-REE-da-tak: sna-CHA-la vaz-MEE za-YAF-koo u klee-YEN-ta, pa-TOM pra-VYER pa-SPART, a DAN-ny-ye vnee-SEE f sees-TYE-moo da kants-TSA DNYA. YEs-lee PA-spar-ta NYET, nee-chee-VO nye a-far-MLYAY — at-DAY za-YAF-koo STRA-she-moo.) The contrast is systematic, not decorative. The spoken procedure names the addressee (слушай, an informal imperative), uses second-person imperatives in the perfective (возьми, проверь, внеси, отдай), fixes no institutional form, and treats the exception as a branch to be handled by a named person (старшему). The written notice names nobody, uses participial and reflexive predicates (не допускается, не разрешается), and encodes its exceptions as nominalised phrases (в случае утери билета). A reader who can move between the two is genuinely in control of the level: the same prohibition 'do not take books out' is Не допускается выносить книги из зала in writing and Не выноси книги из зала, пожалуйста in speech. The second form is not a weaker rule, it is the same rule performed in another register, with a different distribution of responsibility.
depth.mistake: The characteristic error is to treat every obligation word as a synonym and every negative as a prohibition. Three specific traps. (1) Нельзя is not 'forbidden' in all contexts: Cornell's grammar warns it normally takes the imperfective for a standing prohibition, while the perfective describes the impossibility of doing something on one occasion, so Нельзя перейти улицу здесь is a rule and Нельзя перейти улицу сейчас is a fact about traffic. (2) Должен and надо do not put the same noun in the same case: with должен the person is nominative and the subject of the sentence; with надо the person is dative and the sentence has no subject. A learner who writes *Я надо ... or *мне должен has mixed two systems. (3) Согласно governs the dative, so *согласно правил is wrong; the correct form is согласно правилам. Diagnostic procedure: for any obligation sentence, write four labels beside it — who is bound (name and case, or 'nobody named'), what they are bound to do (the infinitive), who has the power to change the sentence (a person, an office, or no one in the text), and which case the governing word requires. If a label cannot be filled in from the text, that is a fact about the text, not a gap in your Russian.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Find one short Russian rule sheet, notice or official instruction of at least five sentences — an airport or metro notice, a library rule, a lease clause, a workplace instruction — and produce two artefacts. Artefact one: a four-column table of obligations, prohibitions, permissions and conditions, with the governing word quoted and its case labelled (dative after согласно, genitive after в случае, dative after разрешается when a person is named). Artefact two: a rewritten spoken version of the same rules addressed to one colleague using вы and perfective imperatives, of at most one hundred words. Model response for the model notice, spoken version: Послушайте, в зал пускают только по билету. Сумки, пожалуйста, оставьте в гардеробе. Еду и напитки сюда не приносите. Книги не выносите без отметки — если что-то нужно, скажите сотруднику. Тишина в зале обязательна, и здесь не курят. Если потеряли билет, обратитесь в администрацию. Self-review rubric, five criteria, one point each: (1) every original obligation appears in the rewrite, and none has been invented; (2) the person bound is explicit in the rewrite and was correctly absent in the original; (3) no prohibition has been silently weakened into a request in either direction; (4) the case government of согласно, в случае and разрешается is correct in the table; (5) your rewrite uses fresh verbs rather than copying the original nominalisations. Reread and repair any row that scored zero. This task is practice, not an examination: nothing here certifies that you can act on a Russian legal or administrative document, and for any decision that carries consequences, use a qualified human reader.
depth.summary: The administrative register is a machine for stating obligations without naming the people who bear them, and it is readable once you know its inventory: impersonal predicatives with a dative person, reflexive passives on -ся, short adjectives that agree with a nominative person, conditional prepositions with fixed case government, nominalised lists, and one emphatic formula, убедительная просьба. The skill transfers to contracts, insurance terms, exam rules and job advertisements, all of which mix the same devices. It also transfers back into production, which is the business of the second unit of this level: if you can read a rule sheet and restate it in speech, you can also write a request, a summary or an argument in the register that a Russian-speaking reader will recognise as correct.

lessons.title: Reading a personal voice: time ordering, discourse markers and irony in first-person prose
lessons.explanation: A first-person text — a blog post, a diary entry, a long letter, a personal essay — is the third large family of real Russian prose, and it is harder than a news report in one specific way: the writer is inside the story, so the text carries two timelines at once, the events and the narrator's changing understanding of them. The vocabulary that manages that second timeline is a small set of discourse markers, and reading them accurately is most of the skill. A story commonly opens with как-то раз (KAK-ta RAS), 'once, one time' — a fixed introductory formula, not the question word как with a particle, so do not translate it as 'somehow'. The narrator's first misunderstanding is often introduced with мне казалось (mnye ka-ZA-las), 'it seemed to me', and its later correction with оказывается (a-KA-zy-va-ye-tsa), 'it turns out', or оказалось (a-ka-ZA-las), 'it turned out' — both of which revise an earlier sentence rather than adding a new event. Suspense inside a personal story is carried by вдруг (VDROOK), 'suddenly', and the resolution by в конце концов (f kan-TSYE kan-TSOF), 'in the end'. One word names the whole object of such a passage — a навык (NA-vyk), 'a skill, an acquired habit', which is what a first-person text about learning usually describes. Two markers signal honesty rather than content: честно говоря (CHES-na ga-va-RYA), 'honestly speaking', which usually introduces an admission that weakens the story, and кстати (KSTA-tee), 'by the way', which introduces an aside. Contrast inside one life is marked by зато (za-TO), 'but on the other hand, in compensation', a conjunction that concedes a loss and points to a gain in the same sentence, and closure by с тех пор (s tyekh POR), 'since then', or не зря (nye ZRYA), 'not for nothing'. Time is expressed with clauses rather than with bare phrases, and here Cornell's grammar gives the usable rule: 'In Russian, clauses must be introduced by clause introducers, not by prepositions.' That is why 'after dinner' is после ужина (a prepositional phrase with the genitive) but 'after he had dinner' must be после того, как он поужинал — a correlative built on того + как. One adverb deserves special care because its meaning depends on tense. Давно (dav-NO) with a past-tense verb means 'long ago': я узнала об этом давно, 'I found out about that long ago'. With a non-past imperfective verb it means 'for a long time now': я давно занимаюсь русским, 'I have been studying Russian for a long time now'. Reading давно as 'long ago' in the second sentence turns a present habit into a finished episode, which is exactly the kind of error that makes a personal text feel incoherent.
lessons.example: Here is an authored first-person passage written for this lesson; it is a teaching text, not a quotation from anyone's diary. Как-то раз, года три назад, я записалась на курсы русского языка. Об этих курсах я знала давно, но записалась только тогда, когда поняла, что мне нужно читать по-русски для работы. Первый месяц мне казалось, что я не понимаю ничего: преподаватель говорил быстро, а я всё время переводила каждое слово. Потом я начала читать вслух по пятнадцать минут в день и через два месяца вдруг обнаружила, что понимаю почти всё. Зато говорить я до сих пор боюсь. Честно говоря, я путаю падежи, кстати, чаще всего в спешке. С тех пор я давно занимаюсь каждый день и уже не перевожу каждое предложение. Не зря говорят, что язык учит привычка, а не память. (KAK-ta RAS, GO-da TREE na-ZAT, ya za-pee-SA-las na KOOR-sy ROOS-ka-va yee-zy-KA. ab EH-teekh KOOR-sakh ya ZNA-la dav-NO, no za-pee-SA-las TOL-ka tag-DA, kag-DA PO-nya-la, shto mnye NOOZH-na chee-TAT pa-ROOS-kee dlya ra-BO-ty. PYER-vy MYE-seets mnye ka-ZA-las, shto ya nye pa-nee-MA-yu nee-chee-VO: pree-pa-da-VA-tyel ga-va-REEL BYST-ra, a ya fsyo VRYE-mya pee-ree-va-DEE-la KAZH-da-ye SLO-va. pa-TOM ya na-CHA-la chee-TAT VLOOK pa peet-NAT-tsat MEE-noot f dyen ee CHYE-ryez dva MYE-sya-tsa VDROOK ab-na-roo-ZHEE-la, shto pa-nee-MA-yu pach-TEE fsyo. za-TO ga-va-REET ya da seeKH POR ba-YU-s. CHES-na ga-va-RYA, ya POO-ta-yu pa-dee-ZHEE, KSTA-tee, CHA-shche fsy-VO f SPYESH-kye. s tyekh POR ya dav-NO za-nee-MA-yu-s KAZH-dy dyen ee oo-ZHE nye pee-ree-va-ZHOO KAZH-da-ye preed-la-ZHE-nee-ye. nye ZRYA ga-va-RYAT, shto yee-ZYK OO-cheet pree-VYCH-ka, a nye PA-meet.) Now read it as three layers rather than one. Layer one, the events, in order: she enrolled three years ago; the first month she understood nothing; she began reading aloud for fifteen minutes; after two months she understood nearly everything; she still fears speaking. Layer two, the narrator's revisions: мне казалось marks the first month as a misapprehension, and вдруг обнаружила marks the change; the word обнаружила, 'discovered', matters because it presents the improvement as something found rather than achieved. Layer three, the narrator's stance towards her own story: зато concedes the cost of the gain, честно говоря admits an ongoing weakness, кстати adds an aside, не зря closes with a generalisation that turns one person's experience into a claim about learning. Notice that два of the sentences are not events at all: я знала давно is background, and я давно занимаюсь is a standing habit described as extending up to now, which is why Russian uses a non-past imperfective. If you read that sentence as past, you turn a habit that is still running into a decision that is over, and the final generalisation then contradicts the text it was meant to conclude.
lessons.question: In the passage above, what work does the word оказывается / оказалось do, and what would be lost if it were deleted?
lessons.answer: It marks a revision of the narrator's earlier understanding — 'it turns out' — so deleting it would leave two contradictory statements (I understood nothing; I understand almost everything) with no signal that the second supersedes the first, and the reader would have to invent the connection.
lessons.distractor: It marks reported speech, because -ся verbs always indicate that someone else's words are being repeated.
lessons.correction: The reflexive ending -ся appears in reporting constructions such as сообщается, but it does not mean 'reported'. In оказалось the -ся belongs to the verb оказаться, 'to turn out', whose meaning is evidential: it presents a fact as newly learned by the speaker. Its function is textual, not grammatical case-work — it tells the reader that the narrative model held until this point is now being corrected. A reader who treats it as reported speech will mis-assign the voice of the sentence to someone else and lose the narrator's own arc, which is the very thing a first-person text is about.

depth.definitions: Discourse markers are words or fixed phrases whose main job is to organise a text rather than to name anything in the world: как-то раз, вдруг, оказывается, зато, кстати, честно говоря, в конце концов, с тех пор. Voice, in this lesson's sense, is the set of linguistic choices that tell you who is speaking and how sure they are: мне казалось, я до сих пор боюсь, не зря говорят. Free indirect discourse is the technique of presenting a character's thought in the narrator's grammatical frame without an introductory verb of saying — a reading skill you need because Russian personal prose uses it for interiority. A time clause is a subordinate clause of time introduced by a clause introducer such as когда or the correlative после того, как, not by a preposition. Prerequisites: the connectors of lesson 46 (и, а, но), cause and result in lesson 47 (потому что, поэтому), когда and если in lesson 48, aspect in narrative in lesson 85, and the reported-speech material of lesson 76, which is what free indirect discourse is the unannounced version of.
depth.mechanism: Why do these markers exist, and why must you not skip them? Because a narrative is not a sequence of true sentences; it is a sequence of sentences together with a constantly changing model of what the narrator knows and believes. Russian marks epistemic changes with small words, and the same story becomes a different story depending on where оказалось sits. Free indirect discourse pushes this further by removing the announcement entirely. As Wikipedia's article on the phenomenon puts it, 'Free indirect discourse differs from indirect discourse in not announcing what it is doing', and it gives the contrast in English: indirect discourse would say 'He feared that he would be late for the party', where free indirect discourse says 'He rummaged through his closet, desperately looking for something suitable to wear. He would be late for the party.' Russian personal prose does the same thing without quotation marks, and the consequence for a reader is that a sentence may belong to two voices at once: a first-person narrator reporting someone else's judgement in her own grammatical frame. There is also an ironic level, which is signalled by nothing at all in the words themselves. Irony in the broad sense described in the encyclopaedia article on the subject arises from 'a contradiction, incongruity, or incompatibility between the two levels' — the level of what is said and the level of what is meant — and it therefore depends on information outside the sentence, such as whether a described day was good or bad. No morphological marker will rescue you; you have to read the whole paragraph to know whether отличный день is praise or complaint.
depth.secondExample: Here is a second authored passage, this time with an ironic surface and a free-indirect moment. Отличный был день! Утром я проспала, потом опоздала на электричку, а на работе выяснилось, что отчёт нужно сдать не в пятницу, а сегодня. Ну да, конечно, я всё успела. Вечером, когда я наконец ехала домой, я думала только о том, что надо менять работу. Кстати, я давно собираюсь это сделать. (at-LEECH-ny byl DYEN! OOT-ram ya pra-SPA-la, pa-TOM a-paz-DA-la na e-lek-TREECH-koo, a na ra-BO-tye VY-ya-snee-las, shto at-CHOT NOOZH-na zdat nye f PYAT-nee-tsoo, a see-VOD-nya. noo da, ka-NYESH-na, ya fsyo oos-PYE-la. VYE-chee-ram, kag-DA ya na-ka-NYETS ye-KHA-la da-MOY, ya DOO-ma-la TOL-ka a tom, shto NA-da mee-NYAT ra-BO-too. KSTA-tee, ya dav-NO sa-bee-RA-yu-s ya EH-ta SDAY-lat.) Three readings, one text. Literal reading: the day was excellent, she was late, the report was due today, she finished everything, and she has long intended to change jobs. Ironic reading: отличный and успела are contradicted by the catalogue of failures and by the final sentence, so the intended meaning is that the day was terrible and nothing was finished — the incongruity is between the evaluation and the facts, exactly the kind of two-level contradiction the article on irony describes. Diagnostic in free-indirect mode: the sentence about changing jobs contains no 'she thought that'; the thought arrives in the narrator's own grammar and would be unmarked if the pronoun were third-person, which is what free indirect discourse does. Notice as well that the day's timeline is carried by clause introducers rather than prepositions — утром, потом, вечером, когда — and that давно собираюсь is a non-past imperfective, so the intention is still alive at the time of speaking, not a closed decision from long ago.
depth.mistake: Three misconceptions recur. (1) Как-то раз is translated as 'somehow' or 'in some way', because the learner recognises как; it actually means 'once, one time' and always opens a specific episode. (2) Давно is always translated 'long ago'; with a non-past imperfective verb it means 'for a long time now', so я давно читаю по-русски is a present habit, and translating it as past makes the next sentence look contradictory. (3) Зато (za-TO) is read as a synonym of но; both contrast, but зато specifically concedes a loss and asserts a compensating gain within the same sentence, which is why it so often sits in the middle of a first-person assessment. A fourth, subtler error is to look for a marker of irony. There is none by design: as the article on irony puts it, the effect depends on 'a contradiction, incongruity, or incompatibility between the two levels', and the levels are in the reader's knowledge, not in the morphology. Diagnostic procedure for a personal passage: write a two-column table of 'what happened' and 'what the narrator now thinks about it', then place every marker in one column or the other. Any marker you cannot place is a word you have not yet read correctly.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Take any first-person Russian text of at least six sentences — a public blog post, a forum answer, a letter you have received — and produce three artefacts. Artefact one: the event timeline as a numbered list, with no commentary. Artefact two: a revision column listing every marker of changing knowledge (оказывается, оказалось, мне казалось, вдруг, в конце концов) and what it revises. Artefact three: one paragraph of English paraphrase that preserves the order of the narrator's discoveries rather than only the order of events. Model response for the model passage: 'Three years ago she enrolled in Russian courses, which she had known about for a long time and joined only when work required reading Russian. During the first month she believed she understood nothing, because she was translating word by word. After she began reading aloud for fifteen minutes a day, she found after two months that she understood nearly everything — a discovery she presents as something that happened to her rather than something she achieved. She still avoids speaking and admits to confusing cases, especially when hurrying, but she now reads daily and no longer translates each sentence; her conclusion is that habit, not memory, teaches a language.' Self-review rubric, four points: (1) no event appears in your timeline that is not in the text; (2) every revision marker from the text appears in your second artefact, with what it revises; (3) your paraphrase does not silently resolve irony into literal meaning; (4) you have kept давно sentences in the tense that Russian gives them. This is a reading exercise; it does not certify comprehension of any particular text or author, and nothing in it is a statement about any real person's private life.
depth.summary: Personal prose is read on two tracks: what happened, and what the narrator now knows. Russian marks the second track with a compact set of discourse markers (как-то раз, вдруг, оказывается, зато, честно говоря, с тех пор), carries interiority into the narrator's grammar through free indirect discourse, and signals irony by contradiction rather than by any word at all. Time inside such a text is managed by clause introducers and by the tense sensitivity of давно. The same inventory is what you will need in order to write: from lesson 96 onwards you will be asked to compress a text without losing its stance, and the markers you have just learned to read are the ones that make compression honest rather than merely short.

lessons.title: Reading numbers and comparison: quantity, rate and the arithmetic behind a claim
lessons.explanation: Russian texts about work, prices, health statistics, budgets and research results are full of numbers, and the numbers are the part most learners read least carefully, because a numeral looks language-independent. It is not: Russian numerals govern cases, mark approximation by word order, and come wrapped in a small vocabulary of comparison whose misuse changes a claim's size by an order of magnitude. Start with the nouns. A процент (pra-TSENT), 'percent', is a unit of rate, and a доля (DO-lya), 'share, proportion', is the same idea expressed as a part of a whole; a text that mixes the two without warning is usually comparing a rate in one year with a share in another. A change can be given in three incompatible ways: на три процента (na TREE pra-TSEN-ta), 'by three percent' — note the preposition на with the accusative; в два раза (v DVA RA-za), 'by a factor of two', which is a different statement from a two-percent change; and the verb составлять (sa-stav-LYAT), 'to amount to, to constitute', which introduces a level rather than a change: доля составила двадцать процентов, 'the share amounted to twenty percent'. Two verbs you will meet beside those nouns are расти (ras-TEE), 'to grow', and снижаться (snee-ZHA-tsa), 'to fall, to decline'. The nouns of movement are рост (ROST), 'growth, a rise', and снижение (snee-ZHEH-nee-ye), 'a decline', and they come with the verb уступать (oos-too-PAT), 'to be behind, to be lower than (something) in some respect' — регион А уступает региону Б по этому показателю. Two hedges are essential to reading honestly. Примерно (pree-MYER-na), 'approximately', and почти (pach-TEE), 'almost', reduce a claim, and they are invisible if you skim: a sentence with почти never supports an exact figure. В среднем (f SRYED-nyem), 'on average', is the most dangerous item in the set, because an average is compatible with an enormous range, and a text that reports only the average has told you nothing about the spread. Russian also lets a writer mark approximation by word order. Cornell's grammar states the rule directly: 'Reversing the order of the numeral and its noun renders the meaning approximately.' So двадцать стаканов is a count of twenty glasses, while стаканов двадцать is 'about twenty glasses'. Finally, case government: after два, три, четыре the noun is genitive singular, after пять and above it is genitive plural, and after numerals ending in один it is nominative singular — a system that Cornell's numerals pages lay out in full. A reader who notices the ending therefore knows whether the text means 'three books' or 'three hundred books' before reaching the noun.
lessons.example: Two short authored statistics paragraphs, and the arithmetic done twice: once as the text states it, once as Russian grammar requires you to read it. Первый текст: В первом полугодии доля семей с детьми в регионе А составила 22,4 процента, а в регионе Б — 19,8 процента. Разница — 2,6 процентного пункта. Примерно каждая пятая семья в регионе А — многодетная. (PYER-vy TYEKST: f PYER-vam pa-loo-GO-dee-ee DO-lya see-MYEY s DYEET-mee f ree-GO-ne A sa-sta-VEE-la DVA-tsat dva za pa-LO-vee-nay PRA-tsen-ta, a f ree-GO-ne B — dee-veet-NAT-tsat VO-seem pa-LO-vee-nay PRA-tsen-ta. RAZ-nee-tsa — dva za pa-LO-vee-nay PRO-tsent-na-va POONK-ta. pree-MYER-na KAZH-da-ya PYA-ta-ya seem-YA f ree-GO-ne A — mna-ga-DYET-na-ya.) Второй текст: За год средняя цена выросла на 6 процентов: с 250 до 265 рублей. В среднем по стране рост составил 5,3 процента, однако почти в половине регионов цены не изменились. (fta-ROY TYEKST: za got SRYED-nya-ya tsee-NA VY-ras-la na SHEST pra-TSEN-taf: s DYES-tee pa-tee-dee-SYAT da DYES-tee sheez-dee-SYAT pa-TEE ROOB-lyey. f SRYED-nyem pa stra-NYE ROST sa-sta-VEEL PYA-ta-ya TREE pra-TSEN-ta, ad-NA-ka pach-TEE f pa-la-VEE-ne ree-GO-naf TSEE-ny nye eez-mee-NEE-lees.) Read the first text with the rate-and-point distinction in mind. The two figures are rates, not counts, and their difference is 2.6 percentage points, which is what процентный пункт (pra-TSENT-ny POONKT) means; writing that difference as a percentage would be wrong, and writing the ratio between the rates as a percentage-point difference would be wrong in the other direction. I checked both readings in code: 22.4 minus 19.8 equals 2.6, so the text's own figure is internally correct, and 22.4 divided by 19.8 equals 1.131313..., so the rate in region A is about 13.1 percent above the rate in region B. Both statements are true and they are not the same statement; a reader who reports only the second one understates how similar the two regions are, and a reader who reports only the first one makes the gap look small. The phrase примерно каждая пятая семья is a hedge plus a fraction, not a count: it means about one family in five multi-child, and any figure derived from it inherits the uncertainty. In the second text, the arithmetic is stated and then immediately qualified. The price rose by 6 percent, and I verified the claim: 265 divided by 250 equals 1.06, so the increase is exactly 6 percent of the original base. The national average of 5.3 percent is compatible with the fact given in the same sentence — almost half the regions did not change their prices at all — because an average can be produced by a minority of large increases. That is the reading a careful reader must perform: the phrase почти в половине регионов не изменились is not decoration, it tells you what the average hides, and it is the kind of sentence that a summary is most likely to lose.
lessons.question: A Russian article says: Цены выросли на 4 процента, а доля семей с кредитами выросла с 40 до 44 процентов. Which statement about the second figure is correct?
lessons.answer: It rose by 4 percentage points, which is also a 10 percent relative increase on the original 40-percent rate, so the two parts of the sentence are describing changes of the same size in points but different sizes in percentage terms.
lessons.distractor: It rose by 4 percent, because the sentence's first clause already established that the change is four percent.
lessons.correction: The first clause belongs to prices and the second to a rate, and the two must be read separately. A rise from 40 to 44 percent is 4 percentage points, and it is also a 10-percent relative increase, because 44 divided by 40 equals 1.10. Wikipedia's article on the percentage point gives exactly this reading of the same numbers: moving up from 40 percent to 44 percent is an increase of 4 percentage points, although it is a 10-percent increase in the quantity being measured if the total amount remains the same. A learner who copies 'на 4 процента' across both clauses has collapsed two different units and will misjudge which change is larger whenever the bases differ.

depth.definitions: A percentage is a number or ratio expressed as a fraction of 100, as Wikipedia's article on percentages puts it: 'a percentage, percent, or per cent (from Latin per centum "by a hundred") is a number or ratio expressed as a fraction of 100'. A percentage point is the unit for the arithmetic difference between two percentages. A share is a percentage treated as a part of a stated whole. A rate is a percentage per unit of time or per unit of population. Average (в среднем, средний) is one summary of a distribution and is silent about spread. Approximation markers are примерно, около, почти, and the inverted numeral order. Case government of numerals: genitive singular after два, три, четыре; genitive plural after пять and up; nominative singular after numerals ending in один. Prerequisites: the counting and quantity material of lesson 45 (сколько, много), comparison in lessons 43-44 (лучше, самый, всех), the singular and plural genitive of lessons 53-54, and the duration constructions of lesson 75 — because time-phrase arithmetic in Russian also distinguishes 'how long it took' from 'how much time was spent'.
depth.mechanism: Why is numerical reading a language skill rather than arithmetic? Because the grammar of a Russian sentence determines which arithmetic is being asserted before you calculate anything, and because a numerical claim's meaning depends on a base that the sentence may leave unstated. The mechanism has four parts. First, unit selection: на plus accusative with a numeral means an absolute change in percentage points unless the noun is the rate word itself, while в плюс a numeral (в два раза, в три раза) means a multiplicative change; the two are not interconvertible without knowing the base. Second, the requirement of a base: a rate of 22.4 percent is meaningless without its denominator, and the average of a distribution is meaningless without the spread, which is why the phrase в среднем must trigger the question 'of what, and with what variation?'. Third, approximation as grammar: the inverted numeral order that Cornell documents means the text itself refuses precision, so any number derived from стаканов двадцать inherits that refusal. Fourth, case as quantity: because the noun ending after a numeral tells you the order of magnitude of the number, a misheard or misread ending can change the quantity by two orders. Two limits should be stated plainly. This lesson teaches you to read and recompute claims; it does not teach statistical inference, and recomputing a figure does not establish that the figure was measured well. And percentages of small bases are unstable: a change from 1 to 2 is a 100-percent increase, which is a true statement about a trivial quantity, and texts that lead with such figures are usually making an argument rather than reporting an amount.
depth.secondExample: Apply the same reading to a comparative sentence with multiplication and a ranking. Продажи выросли вдвое, а средний чек увеличился всего на 8 процентов, поэтому выручка почти не изменилась по сравнению с прошлым годом. По этому показателю компания уступает двум конкурентам примерно на треть. (pra-DA-zhee VY-ras-lee vdvo-YE, a SRYED-nee CHEK oo-vee-LEE-cheel-sya fsy-VO na VO-seem pra-TSEN-taf, pa-EH-ta-moo VY-rooch-ka pach-TEE nye eez-mee-NEE-las pa srav-NYE-nee-yu s PROSH-lym GO-dam. pa EH-ta-moo pa-ka-ZA-tye-lyu kam-PA-nee-ya oos-too-PA-yet dvum kan-koo-RYEN-tam pree-MYER-na na TYERT.) Now unpack it. Вдвое is 'by a factor of two', and it is a multiplier, so a learner who reads it as 'by two' has made an error of 50 percent at least. Средний чек is the average bill, and an 8-percent rise in it together with twice the sales does not add up to flat revenue, so the sentence is asserting a tension the numbers do not obviously support — I checked the direction: if the number of transactions doubles but the average transaction only rises 8 percent, revenue rises by about 8 percent, not by nothing, unless the number of customers is not what doubled. In other words, the word продажи in this sentence is doing a lot of work and the text never tells you whether it counts transactions, units or people. The final clause, уступает двум конкурентам примерно на треть, is a rank plus a hedged proportional gap: being behind by about a third is a relative shortfall, and the ranking construction puts the competitors in the dative plural, since уступать governs the dative. I checked the arithmetic of 'a third' against a worked base: if the leader's figure is 150 and the company's is 100, the shortfall is 50, which is one third of 150 and one half of 100 — so 'behind by a third' is ambiguous until you know whose base is meant.
depth.mistake: The most common error is unit collapse: reading на X процентов as if it meant a relative change of X percent, and reading в X раз as if it meant 'by X'. A second error is treating почти as decoration; почти никогда is 'almost never' and it cancels the exactness of any figure in the same sentence. A third is reading в среднем as a typical value, when it is only a summary that a minority of large values can pull away from the majority, which is exactly what the second model text demonstrates. A fourth, purely grammatical error is ignoring the case after numerals: три книги is three books in the genitive singular, while триста книг is three hundred, and the endings are the only local difference. Diagnostic procedure: for any numerical sentence, write four labels — unit (rate, share, count, duration, money), change type (additive, multiplicative, level), base (explicit or 'not stated'), hedge (none, approximately, almost, on average). Any label you cannot fill from the text is a question the text has left open, and your summary must reproduce that openness rather than closing it.
depth.application: Nonblocking task. Find one Russian text with at least three numbers about a topic you care about — a statistical release, an annual report summary, a news item about prices or health. Do three things. First, reproduce the numbers in a table with the four labels from the diagnostic (unit, change type, base, hedge). Second, recompute every statement of change from its own figures, in code or on paper, and mark each one as confirmed, wrong, or unverifiable for lack of a base. Third, write a fifty-word English summary that preserves every hedge you found. Model response for the second model text: unit — money and rate; change type — additive, 6 percent on a stated base of 250 roubles; base — 250 roubles in the year-earlier price, explicitly given, and the national average has no stated weighting; hedge — 'on average' and 'almost half of the regions'. Recomputations: 265 / 250 = 1.06, so +6 percent confirmed; the claim that the average was 5.3 percent is unverifiable without the regional weights; the claim that almost half the regions were unchanged is a count statement that must be checked against the original table, not against the average. Summary: 'The average price rose by 6 percent, from 250 to 265 roubles, on a stated year-earlier base. The national average rise was 5.3 percent, but the same paragraph reports that prices were unchanged in almost half of the regions, so the average conceals a wide spread; the weighting behind it is not given, and the share of unchanged regions cannot be verified from the average alone.' Self-review rubric, four points: (1) no unit has been converted without showing the arithmetic; (2) every hedge in the source appears in your summary; (3) every 'not stated' base is marked rather than guessed; (4) your own recomputation is shown, not just asserted. Two units of this task can be checked exactly, and they are the only two that can: the arithmetic and the attribution. Everything else is a judgement about a source, not a verification of it.
depth.summary: Numbers in Russian are read twice: once as numerals and once as units, bases and hedges. The grammar of quantity tells you which arithmetic is being asserted — на with the accusative for an additive change, в with a numeral for a multiplicative one, составлять for a level, уступать for a ranking — and the case endings tell you the order of magnitude before the noun arrives. The vocabulary of approximation (примерно, почти, около, the inverted numeral order) and the vocabulary of summary (в среднем) tell you how much the text is claiming, and a careful reader carries all of it into their own summary. This is the last reading lesson of the unit; from here the level turns to production, where the same distinctions have to be built rather than spotted, and where a writer who confuses points with percent will be believed or disbelieved on the wrong grounds.

visual.title: Four-label drill for reading a numerical claim
visual.description: A labelled text diagram: a table with one row per numerical statement and four fixed columns, filled from a source text before any arithmetic is attempted. Rendered as text steps, not as video or animation.
steps: Step 1 — Copy the claim verbatim. Write the Russian sentence exactly, including the hedge, and underline every numeral and every preposition attached to it. Output: the claim as written.
Step 2 — Assign the unit. Mark each numeral as rate, share, count, money or duration, and note whether the preposition is на (additive) or в (multiplicative). Output: a unit label per numeral.

Step 3 — Find the base. Write the denominator, the comparison year or the population group, or the words 'not stated'. Output: a base column in which every unstated base is written as unstated, never guessed.

Step 4 — Recompute and hedge. Do the arithmetic explicitly, record whether the source's own figure is confirmed, and copy every approximation marker into the final column. Output: a checked table plus one sentence stating what the source has not told you.
